bilgi.p1: Topography: LOLA DEM at 10 / 30 / 80 m resolution; permanent shadow (PSR) mask.
bilgi.p2: Illumination: 18.6-year precession cycle; Connecting Ridge 92.27% (2 m) and 95.65% (10 m).
bilgi.p3: Power: 73–117 hours of storage for Shackleton A1; 68 hours when linked to site B 10 km away.
bilgi.p4: Landing safety: slope <8°; at least a 100 m buffer from 8° slopes.
bilgi.p5: Earth / communication: at the pole Earth is above the horizon 48.4% of the time; the uninterrupted window averages 13.1 days and is at most 14.4 days.
bilgi.p6: Gateway: the 9:2 NRHO period averages 6.56 days; it does not determine the mission stay length on its own.
bilgi.p7: DE440: mean lunar radius 1,737.4 km; libration cycle 27.22 days.
bilgi.p_not: These values are regional planning context; they are not results measured at each mission’s site.

ucus.apollo-11.alt: Mare Tranquillitatis • First Crewed Moon Landing
ucus.apollo-11.bilgi: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed in the Sea of Tranquility with the Eagle Lunar Module (LM) and took humanity’s first steps on the lunar surface. They stayed on the surface for 21 hours 36 minutes; 21.5 kg of lunar basalt/regolith was brought back to Earth, and a seismometer and a laser retroreflector (LRRR) were deployed.
ucus.apollo-11.neden: It was chosen because it is a flat basaltic mare floor near the equator, with local slopes under 2°, a very low density of deep craters and boulders that could confuse the landing radar, and a continuous direct communication angle with Earth.
ucus.chandrayaan-3.bilgi: It was the first successful soft landing in history in the Moon’s southern high latitudes (the South Pole region). The Vikram lander and Pragyan rover measured the temperature gradient of the upper regolith near the pole for the first time with the ChaSTE probe and confirmed the presence of sulfur (S), aluminum, calcium and iron in situ with LIBS.
ucus.chandrayaan-3.neden: It was chosen because, although it lies at a high latitude of ~70° S between the Manzinus and Boguslawsky craters, it offers a safe landing plateau of 4.5 × 2.4 km with local slopes under 7°, and provides uninterrupted solar power for a full lunar day (~14 Earth days).
ucus.im1-odysseus.alt: 80.13° S, 1.44° E • Closest Landing to the South Pole
ucus.im1-odysseus.ajans: Intuitive Machines / NASA CLPS • 22 February 2024 • 80.13° S, 1.44° E
ucus.im1-odysseus.bilgi: Launched under NASA’s CLPS program, the Nova-C Odysseus lander touched down at 80.13° S, the closest point to the Moon’s South Pole reached by any spacecraft so far, and was the first US soft landing on the Moon since Apollo 17 in 1972. It carried 6 NASA science payloads to the surface.
ucus.im1-odysseus.neden: It was chosen because it lies next to the 5 km high Malapert Massif, because Earth stays continuously above the horizon there, allowing direct communication, and because it is a gateway to the polar illumination belt for future Artemis bases.
ucus.artemis-shackleton.alt: 89.90° S, 0.00° E • Primary Target at the Exact South Pole
ucus.artemis-shackleton.bilgi_etiket: Planned Landing Target and Mission Profile
ucus.artemis-shackleton.bilgi: Not yet launched; it is target point number 1 for humanity’s first landing at the South Pole (Artemis III) and for our LUNARIS permanent base scenario. The landing is planned on the highly illuminated ridge line that passes through the exact South Pole of the 21 km wide, 4.2 km deep Shackleton Crater.
ucus.artemis-shackleton.neden_etiket: Why Did We Choose This Region?
ucus.artemis-shackleton.neden: According to NASA LOLA/LROC data, it receives sunlight for 85.5–92.1% of the year at a height of 2 m (~45.1 kW of continuous power with a 36 m² panel). The adjacent crater floor is permanently shadowed (PSR, ~40 K) and holds millions of tons of water ice for life support and hydrolysis rocket propellant; the ridge slope is within the <8° safety limit.
ucus.lunaris-connecting-ridge.ajans: Planned Mission (LUNARIS Base Candidate) • 89.40° S, 137.50° W
ucus.lunaris-connecting-ridge.bilgi_etik: Planned Landing Target and Mission Profile
ucus.lunaris-connecting-ridge.bilgi: Not yet launched; it is the strategic target point number 2 that we identified for long-duration autonomous power generation and robotic ice drilling on the ridge (Connecting Ridge) linking the Shackleton and de Gerlache craters.
ucus.lunaris-connecting-ridge.neden_etik: Why Did We Choose This Region?
ucus.lunaris-connecting-ridge.neden: With an average illumination of 92.27% at 2 m and 95.65% at a 10 m tower, it is the region with the longest uninterrupted Sun window on the entire lunar surface. It forms a natural energy bridge exactly between two large permanently shadowed water ice craters (Shackleton and de Gerlache) and meets the <8° slope condition.
